items.title: The most common word in English carries almost no meaning
items.claim: 'The' is the most frequent word in written English, accounting for about 7% of all words in the Brown Corpus. What does it actually contribute?

options.text: It conveys ownership, like a possessive pronoun
It marks definiteness — signalling that the referent is identifiable to the listener, without carrying lexical content itself
It functions as a tense marker for the verb that follows
It is purely decorative and could be omitted without loss of meaning

items.reveal:
'The' is a determiner. It does not refer to anything itself but marks the noun phrase as definite — the speaker assumes the hearer can identify the referent (shared context, prior mention, uniqueness).

Many languages do not have articles at all (Russian, Mandarin, Japanese, Latin). Learners from those languages find English articles famously difficult precisely because the function is grammatical, not lexical.

Function words (the, of, and, to, a) make up roughly half of all word tokens in English running text, but only a tiny fraction of the lexicon.
items.why: Students often think 'meaning' lives in content words. Function words are the structural beams holding sentences together — invisible until you try to remove one.

items.title: Chomsky's 'universal grammar' is contested, not consensus
items.claim: Noam Chomsky has argued for an innate language faculty since the 1950s. What is the state of the debate now?

options.text: It is a settled scientific fact accepted by all linguists
It remains influential but is heavily contested by usage-based, functionalist and connectionist approaches (Tomasello, Everett, Goldberg)
It was disproved by Skinner in the 1970s

items.reveal:
Chomsky's nativism — the claim that humans have an innate, species-specific language faculty with universal grammatical properties — was the dominant paradigm from the 1960s. Daniel Everett's work on Pirahã (a language he argues lacks recursion) challenged a core Chomskyan claim. Michael Tomasello's usage-based approach grounds acquisition in general cognitive learning. Adele Goldberg's construction grammar offers a non-generative model.

No consensus exists. The debate matters for AI, child development, and what counts as 'innate' in human minds.
items.why: Textbooks often present Chomsky as settled fact. He's a major figure with a contested theory. Knowing the debate is part of doing language seriously.

items.title: English pronunciation changed completely between Chaucer and Shakespeare
items.claim: Why does 'name' rhyme with 'fame' (long /eɪ/) when in Chaucer's time it was pronounced 'nah-meh'?

options.text: A gradual French influence after the Norman Conquest
The Great Vowel Shift — a chain reaction in which long vowels raised and diphthongised across English, roughly 1400-1700
Shakespeare deliberately reformed English pronunciation for his plays
The printing press standardised pronunciation by reading instructions in books

items.reveal_title: A chain reaction in the mouth
items.reveal:
Otto Jespersen named the Great Vowel Shift in 1909. Middle English long /aː/ ('ah') raised to /eː/, /eː/ to /iː/, and high vowels /iː/ and /uː/ diphthongised to /aɪ/ and /aʊ/.

This is why English spelling matches pre-shift pronunciation but mouths don't: 'name' was 'nahme', 'meet' was 'mate', 'time' was 'teem', 'house' was 'hoose'. Caxton's printing press (1476) froze spelling roughly mid-shift, leaving the mismatch we live with.

Causes are debated: post-plague demographic mixing, social pressure from emerging middle-class speech, internal phonological pressure.
items.why: English spelling looks broken because it preserves the pronunciation of a language nobody alive speaks. The shift is also why Chaucer is hard to read aloud — you're not just decoding spelling, you're hearing a different sound system.
